trial_050_result.root_cause_found_and_fixed: training_run.py's compute_metrics() computed per-batch recall (tp/(tp+fn)) and averaged those ratios across batches. With batch_size=8 and 383 labels at 3.58% positive rate, the expected positive count for any given label in an 8-example batch is ~0.29 - meaning the overwhelming majority of (label, batch) pairs have zero true positives, so tp/(tp+fn+eps)=0 for most labels in most batches regardless of model quality, dragging every batch's (and therefore the epoch's) averaged recall toward 0. This is a ratio-aggregation error (average-of-ratios != ratio-of-sums), not present for accuracy (a linear average, aggregates correctly regardless of batching) - only recall was affected. Confirmed via a synthetic test: a model constructed to have true recall=1.0 was reported as 25.7% recall under the old per-batch-averaging code, 100% under the fix. Fixed by having compute_metrics() return raw per-batch counts (correct/total/tp/fn) and adding finalize_metrics() to accumulate those across a full epoch before computing the final ratio once - applied to both the training and validation loops. Prior trials (3-label task) were only mildly affected by this bug, since 3 sparse-but-not-this-sparse labels rarely hit zero-positives-per-8-example-batch the way 383 labels do; not worth re-running them retroactively.
trial_050_result.implication: val_loss (never affected by this bug) remains the trustworthy metric across the whole sweep, old and new phases alike. val_recall/train_recall going forward (trial-051+) will now be computed correctly and should be trusted; anything before this fix (all of trial-001 through trial-050) has recall numbers that undersold real model quality on sparse/high-label-count tasks, worst for trial-050 specifically.

pos_weight_feature.why: trial-050's diagnostic showed a real, if moderate, threshold-calibration issue from class imbalance: best F1 (0.5727) came at threshold=0.32, not 0.5, and recall@0.5 was only 45.8% - unweighted BCE naturally pushes predicted probabilities low when negatives vastly outnumber positives (3.58% overall). pos_weight counteracts this by upweighting the loss contribution from positive-label mistakes, per label.
pos_weight_feature.implementation: New --pos-weight flag (BooleanOptionalAction, default False) on training_run.py. When set, computes per-label sqrt(n_negative/n_positive) from the training split's label_counts (already computed for bias-init, now hoisted out of the resume-from-revision conditional so it's always available) and passes it as BCEWithLogitsLoss's pos_weight tensor. sqrt chosen over raw inverse-frequency after checking the real distribution: raw ratio spans 0.38-4780.7 across the 383 labels (~12,600x, would cause gradient spikes whenever a rare positive appears in a batch), sqrt compresses this to 0.61-69.14 (~113x) while staying well-behaved at both ends with no clamp/floor needed (unlike a naive log2 formula, which goes negative for the majority-positive aspect roots). Verified: pos_weight tensor shape/values match the hand-computed distribution exactly, BCEWithLogitsLoss accepts and broadcasts it correctly against [batch, 383] targets, CLI flag parses correctly.

This directly conflicts with the ProtBERT-comparison finding that motivated this phase in the first place (more data exposure mattered) - LoRA solved the VRAM constraint but did NOT solve the compute constraint, since forward/backward FLOPs scale with the full frozen backbone regardless of how few parameters are trainable.

trial_067.unexplained_gap_hypothesis: 138x actual vs ~81x parameter-ratio-only expectation - the remaining ~1.7x is plausibly gradient_checkpointing's recompute overhead (commonly costs ~20-40% more backward-pass compute, trading compute for memory) plus other hardware/kernel-efficiency factors not yet isolated. Given v1/v2 smoke tests showed only ~9.5GB peak VRAM usage against a 22.5GB budget - more than 2x headroom unused - gradient_checkpointing may not even be necessary at this batch size, and turning it off is the most promising, cheap, single-variable lever to test for recovering meaningful throughput before accepting this budget as final.
trial_067.next_step: User chose option (a) --no-gradient-checkpointing, and separately asked whether the frozen backbone could be split off entirely (run once with no gradients, only backprop through a trainable tail) - verified directly against peft 0.19.1 that this is real and implementable via LoraConfig's layers_to_transform (not automatic under the current all-layers-targeted config, matching what the user already expected): restricting adapters to only the last N layers means the earlier layers' output activations have requires_grad=False, so PyTorch's autograd builds no backward graph for them at all. Implemented as --lora-layers-to-transform. Combined both changes into trial-068 (see below) given cost - testing each in isolation wasn't worth the extra 3B-scale spend when both are well-understood in direction.

trial_072.diagnostic_ran_via: experiments/diagnostic_trial072.ipynb (build_diagnostic_notebook.py), run on a cheap GPU per the plan - inference-only, no A100 needed.
trial_072.verdict_vs_trial071_corrected_bar: DECISIVE WIN, clears the corrected bar by a wide margin. Median AUROC: 0.6005 (trial-071) -> 0.8811 (trial-072), a +0.2806 absolute jump (46.7% relative). Expressed as 'skill margin above the 0.5 no-signal baseline' (the fairer way to read this, since AUROC is bounded at 1.0): trial-071's margin was 0.1005, trial-072's is 0.3811 - a 3.79x increase, far beyond what a merely-proportionate or noise-level result would show. Best F1: 0.5319 -> 0.5974 (+12.3% relative). This is the opposite of the red-flag scenario flagged before the trial ran - if --lora-layers-to-transform=10 were capacity-starved, we'd expect the extra ~35.6x data to produce only a marginal or plateauing improvement; instead the model used the extra data very effectively. The capacity concern is resolved: 10 layers of query/value-only LoRA adapters, plus the classifier head, is enough capacity for real, substantial learning on this task, at least up to a 48,000-example training budget.
trial_072.verdict_vs_whole_sweep: BONUS FINDING, not just a win against trial-071: trial-072's median AUROC (0.8811) and best F1 (0.5974) now EXCEED trial-053 (0.8545 / 0.5810), the esm2_t12_35M_coarse_go_terms phase's own best-ever, most-mature result (10 epochs, 12,000 resampled train examples/epoch, 120,000 total exposures - two full beam-search rounds of regularization tuning behind it). trial-072 beats that with under half the total training data (48,000 exposures) and a single 8-epoch trial with zero regularization tuning of its own. trial-072 is now the best-quality checkpoint in this entire sweep, across every phase.
trial_072.cost_honesty_check: This specific comparison (trial-072 vs. trial-053) is a genuine quality win, NOT also a cost win - unlike the earlier trial-072-vs-650M/T4 cost-effectiveness framing. trial-053's 10 epochs at ~574s/epoch = 95.7min at 1x ($ /hr) cost = 1.59 cost-units. trial-072's 57.6min at 5x (A100) cost = 4.80 cost-units - trial-072 cost ~3x more in dollar-normalized terms than trial-053 to produce a better result. The 'this path costs ~5/34 of the alternative' framing from the pivot decision was specifically about 3B/LoRA-on-A100 vs. 650M-full-finetune-on-T4 (still true, and reinforced now that trial-072 beats trial-071 on quality too, not just throughput) - it was never a claim that this path beats the mature 35M/T4 phase on cost, only on quality, which it now demonstrably does.

result.no_oom: Fit comfortably - the memory accounting held up, no fallback needed.
result.vs_trial072_same_data_budget: Essentially a TIE across every metric - median AUROC +0.0054 (+0.61%), mean AUROC +0.0033 (+0.39%), best F1 -0.0003 (-0.05%, technically a hair worse), pooled AUROC +0.0004 (+0.04%), val_loss -0.0002 (-0.30%). Doesn't change the practical conclusion though: whatever the mix of effects, the NET result of going deeper is no meaningful gain at this data budget, at a real throughput cost.
result.verdict: 10 layers is not just the config that fits comfortably - it already captures essentially all the achievable quality at this ~48,000-example data budget. Doubling adapter depth buys nothing here, only costs more. Possible (untested) caveat: capacity differences sometimes only show up with substantially more data than what's been tried - trial-074's much larger 10-epoch/12k-per-epoch run (at layers=10, not 18) won't directly test this, so it remains an open, low-priority question rather than a settled one.

All 3 aspect labels have priors ~70-73% (well above 50%), so the classifier-bias-to-priors init (bias=log(p/(1-p))) starts POSITIVE for every label - every example is predicted 'positive' before any training happens, trivially producing recall=1.0 and ~70% accuracy regardless of whether the model learns anything. Verified precisely: the theoretical entropy floor for 'predict only the prior, zero per-example signal' is 0.5970 (computed from the exact printed priors: H(0.7003)=0.6106, H(0.7257)=0.5875, H(0.7200)=0.5930, mean=0.5970) - the actual final val_loss (0.5950) is statistically indistinguishable from that floor. This is the mirror image of trial-050's original false alarm (there, severe negative imbalance made recall look artificially near-zero despite real learning; here, majority-positive imbalance makes recall look artificially perfect despite near-zero real learning) - exactly why run_diagnostic()'s AUROC exists, and it caught this correctly. No code bug - purely an artifact of the bias-to-priors trick interacting with a >50% base rate, at an extremely small step budget (~88 total optimizer steps across all 4 epochs).

annotation_completeness_investigation.check2_sparsity_correlation: Decisive. Proteins WITH vs WITHOUT each aspect, median total raw GO terms: cellular_component 5.0 vs 2.0; molecular_function 6.0 vs 2.0; biological_process 6.0 vs 1.0. More starkly: 63-75% of proteins missing a given aspect have <=2 total GO terms annotated across their ENTIRE record (vs a full-dataset median of 4). Proteins missing an aspect aren't just missing that aspect - they're systematically under-annotated everywhere, which is what under-studied proteins look like, not what confirmed-absent-function proteins look like.

annotation_completeness_investigation.corollary: Cuts in the model's favor, not against it: trial-080's 0.68 AUROC is scored against ground truth that's partly wrong, so some of the model's apparent false positives are plausibly correct predictions of an aspect Swiss-Prot hasn't gotten around to annotating yet. The 0.68 ceiling likely UNDERSTATES the real biological signal the model learned - it measures agreement with this specific incomplete label set, not a hard ceiling on achievable aspect prediction from sequence.
annotation_completeness_investigation.literature_support: Per user request, checked whether this matches established literature rather than resting on the internal correlation alone. It does, precisely: this is the field's own 'Open World Assumption' for GO annotations. Gaudet & Dessimoz, 'Gene Ontology: Pitfalls, Biases, Remedies' (GO Handbook, Methods in Molecular Biology; also arXiv:1602.01875): 'absence of evidence of function does not imply absence of function... referred to as the Open World Assumption'; a footnote states plainly 'the absence of annotation indicates that no curator has reviewed the literature for this gene product' - the exact mechanism the sparsity correlation above was picking up on. The same source quantifies how rare genuine curator-confirmed negatives are: 'currently less than 1% of all experimental annotations are negative ones [NOT-qualified] in UniProt-GOA' - meaning the overwhelming majority of '0' labels in any GO-derived dataset are absence-of-positive-annotation, not confirmed negatives. It also states the corollary directly: 'overlooking the Open World Assumption can lead to inflated false positive rates in the assessment of gene function prediction tools' - independent confirmation that a model's true AUROC is understated when scored against incomplete ground truth, matching this project's finding without reference to it. Also relevant precedent: CAFA's own time-delayed evaluation design (scoring predictions against annotations that appear after a delay, not the current record) exists specifically because current negatives can't be trusted as ground truth.

pu_learning_discussion.summary: Extended design discussion on how to actually mitigate the OWA problem, not just diagnose it. Covered: (1) IEA/automated annotation transfer (BLAST/GOLabeler-style) - rejected, inherits its own 'propagation bias' (Gaudet & Dessimoz: electronic annotations over-homogenize functional similarity among homologs) and would shrink the negative class further given aspects are already majority-positive; (2) synthetic training data via PLM masked-residue infilling - rejected, doesn't address label reliability at all (only adds assumed positives), real circularity/model-collapse risk (Shumailov et al., Nature 2024) from using ESM to generate training data for an ESM classifier, and would amplify rather than correct the well-studied-protein bias; (3) full nnPU (Kiryo et al. 2017 non-negative PU risk estimator, building on Elkan & Noto 2008) - the mathematically precise answer to 'transfer from valid data, ignore-but-counterbalance unknowns, no free predict-everything-positive collapse', verified via the actual formula (R_pu = pi_p*R_p+ - pi_p*R_p- + R_u-, clamped at 0) but requires a trustworthy true class prior pi_p, which we have no good way to estimate (our observed ~70-73% positive rate is itself an OWA-contaminated underestimate) - deferred as a possible follow-up once there's a health check to calibrate pi_p against; (4) PU-GO (2024, arXiv/PMC) - real, directly relevant published work solving exactly this problem for GO prediction via a ranking loss + ontology-structure-derived priors, but their own ablation shows only modest gains (Fmax +4.7%, AUC +2.1%) for real implementation effort.
pu_learning_discussion.decision: Implemented the simplest, lowest-risk option: masking. Excludes 'negative' labels from the loss (both training and validation-for-best-checkpoint-selection) when the protein's total_terms <= threshold (2, per the investigation), while always trusting positives. Sidesteps needing to estimate pi_p entirely. See trial_081.

round_1.batch_size_finding: Bigger batch (128) gave the sweep's best val_loss despite ~94 opt steps/epoch (16x fewer than batch=8's 1500), but did NOT speed up wall-clock - batch=8 ran ~530-540s/epoch, batch=32 ~680s/epoch, batch=128 ~735s/epoch, the opposite of the usual larger-batch-is-faster expectation. Likely cause (code-level, not batch-size-inherent): data_collate_function pads each batch to its own longest sequence with no length-bucketing, and shuffle=True draws batches randomly - larger batches have a higher chance of containing a near-max_length (1024) outlier, forcing more padding waste as batch size grows. Not fixed as part of this round; would need length-bucketed batching in training_run.py to actually test batch size's effect on throughput cleanly.
round_1.gpu_memory_observations: User reports trial-033 (batch_size=128, grad_accum_steps=1) almost OOM'd the T4; trial-034 (batch_size=128, grad_accum_steps=4, run immediately after) was surprisingly easier on memory. Per training_run.py (create_esm/DataLoader), grad_accum_steps does NOT reduce per-step batch size - the DataLoader batch_size is used as-is every micro-step, so trial-034 processes full batches of 128 exactly like trial-033; the code gives no mechanism for grad_accum alone to lower peak memory. Most likely explanation: CUDA's caching allocator already expanded its pool to fit batch=128 during trial-033, so trial-034 (running right after, same session) reused that already-grown pool instead of needing to allocate further - an artifact of run order within one session, not a real property of grad_accum_steps. Don't read 'higher grad_accum = lower memory' as a real effect without a controlled A/B (same batch size, accum vs no-accum, in fresh sessions on both sides).

True-path-rule-aware loss/label propagation: exploit the GO DAG so rare specific terms borrow gradient signal from their much more frequent ancestors

results.interpretation: AUROC is clearly above 0.5 for every aspect (0.61-0.68, macro 0.64) - the model has learned real per-protein discriminative signal, not just the label prior. This resolves the 'is it a dead end' question from before: it's not. Nuance worth keeping in mind though: at the standard 0.5 threshold, F1 doesn't clearly beat the trivial baseline (and is slightly worse for F/P) - AUROC (ranking ability, threshold-independent) and F1-at-a-fixed-threshold tell different stories here, because F1 rewards the trivial baseline's perfect recall in a way that undersells the model's real but modest ranking improvement. accuracy/recall alone (the only two metrics compute_metrics() has ever tracked) would never have surfaced this - they sat right on top of the trivial baseline the whole sweep, which is exactly why this diagnostic was worth running before deciding whether Stage 1 was usable.

ancestor_propagation_check.method: 500 randomly sampled proteins (seed=42) from train_terms.tsv; for each, computed the full true-path ancestor closure of its listed terms via networkx over the obonet-parsed go-basic.obo graph, then checked what fraction of that closure is already present as explicit rows for that protein.
ancestor_propagation_check.result: Only 2.27% of implied ancestor annotations (450 of 19,813) are already explicit in train_terms.tsv; 97.73% are missing. Every single sampled protein (500/500) had at least one missing ancestor annotation; mean per-protein missing fraction was 98.2%.
ancestor_propagation_check.conclusion: train_terms.tsv lists close to only the most-specific asserted annotations, not the propagated closure. Ancestor propagation (via the obonet graph) is NOT optional for any term-level label space - without it, virtually every candidate depth<=2 term (see real_task_stats) would have its positive examples massively undercounted, since most proteins' coarse-level annotations exist only implicitly through their deeper, more specific terms.

findings: go-basic.obo has 5 relationship types: is_a (62,410 edges), part_of (6,597), regulates (2,989), positively_regulates (2,619), negatively_regulates (2,614). Only is_a/part_of support the true-path rule (regulates does not mean is-a-kind-of/part-of) - restricting propagation to those two changes the ancestor-completeness result only marginally (97.65% missing vs. 97.73% with all 5 edge types), but is still the methodologically correct restriction going forward.
0 of 26,125 terms used in train_terms.tsv are missing/obsolete relative to this go-basic.obo - fully version-consistent, no ambiguity from a stale ontology file.
0 of 77,229 edges cross between the C/F/P namespaces - the 3 aspects stay cleanly disjoint.

Depth is convention-dependent: shortest-path vs longest-path depth disagree for 61% of a 2000-term sample, by 1.73 levels on average, up to 10 in the worst case. The ancestor/descendant SET itself is exact and deterministic once edge types are fixed - only the scalar 'depth' summary is ambiguous. Resolved by committing explicitly to shortest-path depth throughout.
